source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, Photograph of the crowd outside the New York Stock Exchange, October 29, 1929, public domain.
stem: The crowd in the photograph most directly reflects which of the following?

options.text: Panic among investors as stock prices collapsed in October 1929.
Celebration of the opening of the New York Stock Exchange’s new building.
options.misconception: No one celebrates a crash; the crowd gathered because prices were collapsing, not for an opening.

options.text: A protest demanding that the federal government create the Federal Reserve.
options.misconception: The Federal Reserve already existed, created in 1913, so no one needed to demand it in 1929.

options.text: Workers gathering for a parade celebrating the end of World War I.
options.misconception: The war had ended eleven years earlier, in 1918, and this crowd is on Wall Street, not at a parade.

rationales.A: October 29, 1929, was Black Tuesday, the crash’s worst day. The crowd on Wall Street is investors and onlookers reacting to prices in free fall.
rationales.B: No one celebrates a crash. The crowd gathered because prices were collapsing, not for a building opening.
rationales.C: The Federal Reserve already existed, created in 1913. No one needed to demand it in 1929.
rationales.D: The war had ended eleven years earlier, in 1918. This crowd is on Wall Street, not at a parade.
rationales.general:
1. Read the date. October 29, 1929, is the day of the crash, known as Black Tuesday.
2. Look at the crowd. Hundreds of people pack Wall Street outside the Exchange.
3. Ask why a crowd gathers at a stock exchange. People come when their money is at stake.
4. Put it together. The photograph catches panic in the act, on the worst day of the crash.
Remember: a photograph’s date is often the whole answer. Anchor the image in its day first.
